newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Cut in NZ wool exports to China seen long-term.
newsitem.headline: Cut in NZ wool exports to China seen long-term.

text.p: A plunge in New Zealand wool exports to China this year is seen as a long-term trend, a leading New Zealand exporting body said on Monday.
Wool Services International Managing Director Michael Dwyer said the Chinese had shown a "huge jump" in preference for finer wools that New Zealand could not easily supply.
China took 39 percent of New Zealand's wool in the year to June 30, 1996 but its buying has been down 29 percent in the eight months of the season this year against last season.

"China is pivotal because they have been buying over 30 percent of all our wool," Dwyer said. "If you get that dropping to something like 20 percent, it has a major impact on the price of your fibre."
Beijing had turned to Australia and Uruguay, resulting in a 60 percent drop in New Zealand exports to China in the first two months of 1997 compared with the same months in 1996, he said.
Jeff Jackson, chairman of the farmer cooperative overseeing the New Zealand industry, Wools of New Zealand (WNZ), is flying to China on Tuesday to investigate possible problems.

WNZ Corporate Relations Manager Roger Buchanan, also going to China, was reluctant to discuss problems ahead of the trip but said it was a "rather sweeping statement" to say the fall-off in Chinese exports was long-term.
"We'd prefer not to be adding to the debate. Obviously some of the reports coming out are of concern and we want to get a better fix on just what some of the issues are."
Buchanan said WNZ wanted to investigate reports about the quality of New Zealand's product, the dynamics of changes in the market and to more clearly understand government policies.
WNZ had predicted for a long time that the China wool market would progressively move towards finer wools as it evolved from predominantly hand-knitted to machine-knitted products.
Dwyer said the reason for the falloff was a drop in carpet production as the Chinese government reduced its exposure to state-owned mills as a result of their losses last year.
There had also been a switch from the coarser wools produced by New Zealand and used in hand knitting yarns to machine knitted clothes for which finer wool is required.
"It's a fashion change," Dywer said.
He said New Zealand needed to find new uses for its wools and to speed up development of different processing and manufacturing options.
Dywer said 60 percent of New Zealand wool was used for carpet production and carpets had become a commodity like wool.
A current research project on developing a cotton and wool blend carpet made a lot of sense, he said.

Council of Wool Exporters President Don Quested described current overall wool market conditions as static despite the recent improvement in prices for finer micron wools such as merino and halfbred fleece.
He said it was getting extremely difficult to shift this season's increased volumes of stronger micron wools which had come about because of good summer and autumn growing conditions.
"There is a greater amount of wool measuring 40 microns and stronger available this year. Unfortuneately buyers are showing less and less interest in these coarser wool types."

Quested said the most positive development in the market was the lack of stockpiled wool. Any increase in demand would be good for prices with no huge stockpile of wool sitting around for buyers to dip into if and when demand picked up.
